rationale: A wins because it keeps the tension honest and beat-shaped: "Oatly cuts the carbon footprint of its barista oat milk by 31% while closing a US plant" is a real business story, not a garnish on a product launch. B has useful parts, but "customers who don't specify get oat milk" is a bad misread of "default non-dairy option"; that is exactly how a pitch walks into traffic. A still has a sloppy upcharge overreach, but its proof demands and refused angles show adult supervision.
gaps_in_A: "A 1,400-store coffee chain makes oat milk the default, not the upcharge" overstates the facts. The update says default non-dairy option, not no surcharge at the coffee chain.

"Reformulations usually travel with a price move in one direction or the other" is asserted without evidence. The no-price-change fact is useful, but this needs cost or margin proof before it becomes a story.

"The prevailing belief is that unprofitable plant-based companies retreat from sustainability spending when they cut costs" may be true, but it is imported context, not supplied fact. Treat it as a hypothesis unless backed by coverage.
The foodservice angle depends almost entirely on "the chain named and willing to be named." A should flag that as a gate before calling the angle viable, not just a proof item.
gaps_in_B: "customers who don't specify get oat milk" is wrong on the supplied facts. "Default non-dairy option" does not mean oat milk replaces dairy as the default for every drink.
"falling volumes, shrinking retail shelf space, canceled expansions" invents a sector narrative not present in the update. If you need all that scaffolding, your angle is not grounded enough yet.
"one of its larger US distribution wins" is unsupported. The update gives 1,400 locations, not Oatly's ranking of distribution wins.

It refuses "Customer-story (the coffee chain's procurement decision)" as `no_journalist_shape` while leading with the same chain-as-protagonist angle. That is not rigor; that is the model forgetting what it just wrote.
